name: Gugu-Yalanji
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: Stress, which is characterised by higher pitch and loudness (cf. Ladefoged 1975:222ff), identifies a word as a unit in Kuku Yalanji. Clausal intonation contours, the highest point of which is the clause stress, show some variation and are the only distinguishing feature for certain types of clauses.
sweep_summary: Kuku-Yalanji (kuku1273), catalog fixed-strict (initial primary only, window 2-8). this search of works with stress in the title's single title hit, Hershberger & Pike 1970 'Stress as related to the grammar of Gugu-Yalanji' (PL C-13:791-810), was already held by the project with a text and was read: p. 791 'Word stress occurs on the first syllable of words', characterised by loudness and highest pitch, words 2-8 syllables; p. 792 optional secondary on the first syllable of the second stem in reduplications/compounds, present in slow speech only; clause stress is a separate layer that co-occurs with word stress. Confirms the catalog. I also downloaded the catalog's deciding source, Patz 2002 (PL 527, ANU repository, open PDF + text, saved), and read §2.6-2.6.1 pp. 35-36: 'Every word in Kuku Yalanji has primary stress on the first syllable', secondaries non-obligatory and morphology-anchored, 'in normal speech.. only the first syllable is stressed'. Confirms; the record's deciding quotation is the §2.6 intro sentence and would be better served by the §2.6.1 placement sentence (same source, no supersession). Oates & Oates 1964 (the origin of the survey chain's 'penult secondary', the compilers note's remaining pin) exists as two controlled-lending scans on archive.org; full text could not be reached by automated download and inside-search 'Item not available', so it stays unread (low priority, historiographic only). No contradiction found; no other stress-titled work for this language surfaced in the Glottolog/Semantic Scholar/Crossref title search.org's API instead.

new_statements.quote: Every word in Kuku Yalanji has primary stress on the first syllable, after which there is a distinct drop in pitch for disyllabic words and a more gradual drop for words of more than two syllables (see Hershberger & Pike 1970:791-792). Words with four or more syllables that are roots, reduplicated forms, or compounds, may have secondary stress on the third syllable, that is the first syllable of the second root in reduplicated forms of compounds. [...] However, secondary stress is not obligatory and is usually omitted in other than careful citation forms, leaving the word with stress only on the first syllable.

new_statements.reading: Fixed initial primary stress on every word, weight-blind, up to 8 syllables; secondaries are optional, careful-speech, morphology-anchored (never a count-computable penult rule). This is exactly the catalog's reclassified rule (initial only, window 2-8, fixed-strict). Hershberger & Pike 1970:791-792 (this search of works with stress in the title's one title hit, held by the project and read) says the same: 'Word stress occurs on the first syllable of words', secondary on the first syllable of the second stem in slow speech only. Patz 2002 is already the catalog's deciding source, so nothing supersedes; the one refinement worth carrying is that the deciding quotation on the record (the §2.6 opening sentence about stress identifying the word as a unit) should be replaced or supplemented by the §2.6.1 placement sentence quoted here, which states where stress falls.

Words with four or more syllables that are roots, reduplicated forms, or compounds, may have secondary stress on the third syllable, that is the first syllable of the second root [...] However, secondary stress is not obligatory and is usually omitted in other than careful citation forms, leaving the word with stress only on the first syllable.
sources.note: Exceptionless initial primary stress; optional secondaries (careful speech only) anchored to root/suffix boundaries — third syllable in 4+-syllable roots/reduplications/compounds, suffix-initial for disyllabic suffixes, penult in >3-syllable words with monosyllabic suffixes/clitics unless the penult is the last root syllable; -baja-ku never stressed. p. 36: 'In normal speech, even in long words of up to eight syllables, only the first syllable is stressed'. Patz states her findings concur with Hershberger & Pike 1970. The catalog_quote carried on the record is the §2.6 opening sentence (p. 35…

sources.citation: Hershberger, Henry & Eunice V. Pike. 1970. Stress as related to the grammar of Gugu-Yalanji. In S.A. Wurm & D.C. Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell (Pacific Linguistics C-13), 791-810. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C13.791 (CC BY-SA 4.0, ANU Open Research handle 1885/253842).
sources.quote: p.791: 'Word stress occurs on the first syllable of words. It is characterised by loudness and the highest pitch of the word. A word has a minimum of two syllables, but may have as many as eight. In words of two syllables there is a sharp drop in pitch between the two syllables'. p.792: 'Certain words (usually those with reduplicated stems, but occasionally those with compound stems) have a secondary stress which occurs on the first syllable of the second stem. There is variation in the occurrence of this secondary stress in that it usually occurs in slow speech but may be lacking in fast spee
sources.note: Primary word stress fixed on the first syllable of every word (2-8 syllables), cued by loudness and highest pitch. An optional secondary stress falls on the first syllable of the second stem in reduplications/compounds, present in slow speech and often absent in fast speech; it is stem-anchored, never penult-anchored. Clause stress (§2, p. 792) is a separate, higher-level prominence that 'occurs on the first syllable of a word, that is, it co-occurs with word stress'. Nothing weight-sensitive anywhere.

tone.quote: The symbol ° indicates declarative clause stress. The symbol " indicates interrogative clause stress--extra high pitch on the syllable marked. The following symbols will be used for intonation: (1) /./ = termination intonation--from the last stress there is a downstep of pitch with decrescendo on each syllable successively. (2) /,/ = sequence intonation--an upstep of pitch on the last syllable. (3) /;/ = tentative pause intonation--similar to termination intonation except that it does not end as low and the downstep is not as steep or relaxed. (4) /:/ = call intonation--the last syllable starts extra high and glides downward.
